chunks: Abu Hanifa came to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him). He (AS) said to him: 'O Abu Hanifa! It has reached me that you practice qiyas.' He said: 'Yes.'
He (AS) said: 'Do not practice qiyas, for indeed the first to use analogy was Iblis, when he said:'
'You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.'

So he analogised between fire and clay. Had he compared the luminous nature (nuriyya) of Adam with the luminous nature of fire, he would have recognised the superiority between the two lights and the purity of one over the other.

key_terms.تَقِيسُ: practice qiyas — analogical reasoning used in deriving juristic rulings by comparing analogous cases
key_terms.صَفَاءَ: safa' — purity, clarity; the refined, unmixed excellence of one light over another
key_terms.فَضْلَ: fadl — superiority, excellence; the hierarchical precedence of one thing over another
key_terms.نُورِيَّةَ: nuriyya — luminous/spiritual nature, inner radiance; a term denoting the essential metaphysical quality of a being

ai.seo_question: Why does Imam al-Sadiq (AS) prohibit qiyas (analogical reasoning) and what does the example of Iblis teach about the dangers of superficial comparison in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) forbids Abu Hanifa from using qiyas (analogical reasoning in jurisprudence), tracing the origin of this method to Iblis, who compared his fiery substance to Adam's clay and concluded his own superiority. The Imam argues that Iblis's fatal error was in choosing the wrong basis for comparison: had he measured Adam's spiritual luminosity (nuriyya) against the luminosity of fire, he would have perceived Adam's manifest excellence — demonstrating that superficial analogy obscures deeper spiritual realities.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ahmad Bin Abdullah Al Aqeely, from Isa Bin Abdullah Al Qurshy who said, 
‘Abu Haneefa came over to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, so he<sup>asws</sup> said to him: ‘O Abu Haneefa! It has reached me<sup>asws</sup> that you tend to analogise?’ He said, ‘Yes’.
He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Do not analogise, for the first one who analogised was Iblees<sup>la</sup> where he<sup>la</sup> said
[38:76] He said: I am better than him; You have Created me from fire, and Created him from clay.

So he<sup>la</sup> analogised what was between the fire and the clay, and had he<sup>la</sup> compared Adam<sup>as</sup> with the radiance of the fire, he<sup>la</sup> would have recognised what is between the two radiances and the excellence of one of the two upon the other’.
en.sarwar: 20. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Ahmad ibn ‘Abdallah al-‘Aqili from ‘Isa ibn ‘Abdallah al-Qurashi who has said the following. “Once abu Hanifah came to see Imam abu ‘Abdallah (a.s.) who said to abu Hanifah, “O abu Hanifah, do you practice analogy as I hear you do?” Abu Hanifah replied, “Yes, I do practice analogy.”
The Imam then said to him, “Do not practice it because the first person who used analogy was Satan when he said, “
Lord, you have created me from fire and created him from clay.”
He analogized fire with clay. If he would have analogized the light in the clay and fire he would have learned about the difference between the two lights and the excellence of one over the other.”
